source_text:
Ex homiliis in epistulam ad Hebraeos
14.1308 Ὁ χαρακτὴρ τῆς λέξεως τῆς πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπιγεγραμμένης Ἐπιστολῆς οὐκ
ἔχει τὸ ἐν λόγῳ ἰδιωτι 14.1309 κὸν τοῦ Ἀποστόλου, ὁμολογήσαντος ἑαυτὸν ἰδιώτην
εἶναι τῷ λόγῳ, τουτέστι, τῇ φράσει. Ἀλλὰ ἐστὶν ἡ Ἐπιστολὴ συνθέσει τῆς λέξεως
ἑλληνικωτέρα, πᾶς ὁ ἐπιστάμενος κρίνειν φράσεων διαφορὰς, ὁμολογήσαι ἄν· πάλιν
τε αὖ ὅτι τὰ νοήματα τῆς ἐπιστολῆς θαυμάσιά ἐστι, καὶ οὐ δεύτερα τῶν ἀποστολικῶν
ὁμολογουμένων γραμμάτων, καὶ τοῦτο ἂν συμφήσαι εἶναι ἀληθὲς πᾶς ὁ προσέχων
τῇ ἀναγνώσει τῇ ἀποστολικῇ.
thought_title: The polished style of Hebrews compared with Paul's plain speech
orientation: Origen opens his homily on Hebrews by comparing the epistle's Greek style with Paul's admitted plainness of speech.
pass_a_gloss: The style of the Epistle inscribed to the Hebrews does not have the untrained-in-speech quality of the Apostle, who confessed himself to be untrained in speech, that is, in wording. But the Epistle is more Greek in the composition of its wording; everyone who knows how to judge differences of wording would agree. And again, that the thoughts of the epistle are wonderful and not second to the acknowledged apostolic writings, this too everyone who attends to the apostolic reading would agree is true.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'style' for this phrase, referring to the distinctive character of the wording.
This noun form corresponds to the glossary term 'untrained in speech' for Paul's self-description, preserving the quality sense.
The glossary requires 'wording' for φράσις, distinguishing it from thoughts.
The glossary requires 'composition' for σύνθεσις, and 'wording' for λέξις, keeping the distinction from thoughts.
The glossary requires 'thoughts' for νοήματα, the ideas contained in the epistle.

pass_b_english: The Epistle to the Hebrews does not have the Apostle's untrained-in-speech quality in its style, even though he confessed that he was untrained in speech—that is, in wording. Rather, anyone who knows how to judge differences in wording would agree that the epistle is more polished in Greek style in the composition of its wording. And again, anyone who attends to the apostolic reading would also agree that this is true: the thoughts of the epistle are wonderful and not second to the acknowledged apostolic writings.
